:::{.def}

We already saw that before images reach a model, they must be transformed into tensors with uniform size and data type, and values in a sensible range. On top of this, randomly perturbing the training images (augmentation) is a cheap way to get more out of a small dataset and prevent overtraining.

:::

## Setup

```{python}
import torch
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset
from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT
from torchvision.transforms import v2 as T

torch.manual_seed(42)
```

As before, we reload the dataset and [the split saved earlier](pt2_datasets.qmd), and pick one training image to work on:

```{python}
eurosat = EuroSAT(root="data")
idx = torch.load("data/split.pt", weights_only=True)
img, label = eurosat[idx["train"][0]]
print(type(img).__name__, img.size, "->", label, eurosat.classes[label])
```

## The validation pipeline

A model needs every input as a float32 tensor of the same shape, with values in a comparable range. For evaluation, this conversion must be deterministic. Here is the whole pipeline for our validation images:

```{python}
IMAGENET_MEAN = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406]
IMAGENET_STD = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]

val_tf = T.Compose([
    T.ToImage(),                           # PIL image -> uint8 CHW tensor
    T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),  # /255 -> float32 in [0, 1]
    T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD),
])
```

Let's run the three stages one by one on our image:

```{python}
x = T.ToImage()(img)
print(x.shape, x.dtype, int(x.min()), int(x.max()))
```

- [`T.ToImage()`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.ToImage.html) turns the PIL image into a uint8 tensor of shape (3, 64, 64): channels first, the layout PyTorch expects.
- The values are raw pixel intensities from 0 to 255.

```{python}
x = T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)(x)
print(x.shape, x.dtype, f"{x.min():.3f} {x.max():.3f}")
```

- [`T.ToDtype`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.ToDtype.html) with `scale=True` rescales to [0, 1] while converting to float32, the data type models compute in.

```{python}
x = T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD)(x)
print(x.shape, x.dtype, f"{x.min():.2f} {x.max():.2f}")
```

```{python}
print([f"{v:+.2f}" for v in x.mean(dim=(1, 2)).tolist()])
```

- [`T.Normalize`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.Normalize.html) standardizes each channel: it subtracts a mean and divides by a standard deviation.

Why these particular mean and std? They are the per-channel statistics of ImageNet, the dataset the pretrained models of a later section were trained on: those models expect inputs normalized exactly this way. We adopt them for the whole course, including our from-scratch baseline, so that every run stays comparable.

:::{.note}

Our Forest patch normalizes to channel means of about −1.01, −0.65, and +0.11: far from zero. EuroSAT is darker and greener than the average ImageNet photo. When training a model from scratch, computing your own dataset statistics is a legitimate choice; what matters is using the same statistics everywhere, data and model consistent.

:::

:::{.note}

Older tutorials use `transforms.ToTensor()`: the v2 equivalent is `ToImage()` followed by `ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)`.

:::

Two things are missing from this pipeline that you will usually need for your own data. EuroSAT images are all 64 × 64 pixels, so there is no [`T.Resize`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.Resize.html); and evaluation crops are deterministic, so there is no random crop. For mixed-size images, the standard evaluation recipe is `T.Resize(256)` followed by [`T.CenterCrop(224)`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.CenterCrop.html).

## The training pipeline

The file count of a small dataset is fixed, but the model should not keep seeing the exact same pixels. **Augmentation** applies random, label-preserving changes to training images at every read: the model then never trains on the same tensor twice and cannot rely on accidents of orientation or framing.

```{python}
train_tf = T.Compose([
    T.ToImage(),
    T.RandomHorizontalFlip(),  # p=0.5 by default
    T.RandomVerticalFlip(),    # p=0.5 by default
    T.RandomRotation(90),      # random angle in [-90, 90]
    T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),
    T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD),
])
```

Why these three transforms? Satellite images look straight down: there is no "up" in a nadir view, and a field, a highway, or a lake flipped or rotated is still the same class. This reasoning is domain-specific: rotating handwritten digits would turn some 6s into 9s, and flipping text left to right destroys it. Every augmentation you add is a bet that the change preserves the label of every image in the dataset.

The random transforms sit before the dtype conversion: geometry on uint8 tensors is cheaper than on float32, and `Normalize` must come last.

Here is one image (a highway) next to seven passes of the random part of the pipeline:

```{python}
aug_display = T.Compose([           # for screens: without Normalize
    T.ToImage(),
    T.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
    T.RandomVerticalFlip(),
    T.RandomRotation(90),
])

img, label = eurosat[10000]
print(label, eurosat.classes[label])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(10.5, 5.5))
axes.flat[0].imshow(img)
axes.flat[0].set_title("original", fontsize=9)
axes.flat[0].axis("off")
for ax in axes.flat[1:]:
    ax.imshow(aug_display(img).permute(1, 2, 0))  # CHW -> HWC
    ax.axis("off")
```

Every call draws fresh random parameters:

```{python}
a, b, c = train_tf(img), train_tf(img), train_tf(img)
print(torch.equal(a, b), torch.equal(b, c))
```

Our 21,600 training files now yield effectively unbounded distinct training tensors: after 10 epochs, the model has seen each file 10 times, but never the same tensor twice.

And the validation transform, being deterministic, returns the identical tensor every time:

```{python}
a, b = val_tf(img), val_tf(img)
print(torch.equal(a, b))
```

[Validation and test transforms must be deterministic.]{.emph} Random transforms at evaluation time add noise to your metrics and let luck masquerade as performance. Augmentation is a training-time tool.

## Where transforms run

Both pipelines attach to the dataset at construction, through the `transform=` argument used in [the DataLoaders section](pt2_dataloaders.qmd). torchvision datasets take it, and so does the custom `ImageFiles` class [we wrote earlier](pt2_datasets.qmd): `transform` was the hook left open for exactly this.

The transform runs inside `__getitem__`, once per sample, therefore inside the worker processes: augmentation is parallelized by the DataLoaders for free. It is not free though: on this machine, one pass over the training set with 4 workers took 2.0 s without augmentation and 4.8 s with flips, rotation, and normalization. Cheap transforms keep the workers ahead of the accelerator; expensive ones starve it again, which is the diagnosis of the previous section.

## One draw per call

The v2 transforms also accept batches of tensors. But watch out: a transform draws one set of random parameters per call, so the whole batch gets flipped or rotated together:

```{python}
batch = torch.stack([T.ToImage()(eurosat[i][0]) for i in range(8)])
hflip = T.RandomHorizontalFlip()
for _ in range(4):
    out = hflip(batch)
    print([not torch.equal(out[i], batch[i]) for i in range(8)])
```

Every line is all `True` or all `False`: never a mix. Per-sample randomness must therefore happen on the dataset side, one `__getitem__` at a time, as we have set up. Batched calls remain useful for deterministic transforms such as `Normalize`.

## When augmentation helps

Augmentation is regularization: it trades easy fit on the training set for generalization.

- **Training from scratch on a small dataset** (our situation in the next section): augmentation is one of the highest-value additions. The model cannot memorize exact images, and validation accuracy typically climbs once the model starts overfitting.
- **Fine-tuning a pretrained model** (a later section of this course): the backbone was already trained on millions of heavily augmented images, so it arrives robust. Start with light or no augmentation; add some back if the gap between training and validation performance grows.
- Every transform must be label-preserving **and** representative of real variation. Photometric jitter on satellite images deserves care: colour carries physical signal there (vegetation, water). Geometric flips and rotations are the safe choice for EuroSAT.

Expect the training loss to fall more slowly with augmentation: the task got harder, not the model worse. Judge on validation metrics.

For a quick strong default on natural images, torchvision also ships one-liner policies such as [`T.TrivialAugmentWide`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.TrivialAugmentWide.html) and [`T.RandAugment`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.RandAugment.html), which compose random transforms for you.

## The complete data pipeline

The data side of the course is now complete: datasets with the right transform per split, loaders with the options measured in the previous section.

```{python}
train = Subset(EuroSAT(root="data", transform=train_tf), idx["train"])
val = Subset(EuroSAT(root="data", transform=val_tf), idx["val"])
print(len(train), len(val))
```

```{python}
loader_kwargs = {
    "batch_size": 64,
    "num_workers": 4,
    "persistent_workers": True,
    "pin_memory": torch.accelerator.is_available(),
}
train_loader = DataLoader(train, shuffle=True, **loader_kwargs)
val_loader = DataLoader(val, **loader_kwargs)
```

One training batch:

```{python}
x, y = next(iter(train_loader))
print(x.shape, x.dtype, f"{x.min():.2f} {x.max():.2f}")
print(y[:8].tolist())
```

Augmented, normalized, shuffled batches of tensors now flow at steady state. What is still missing is the model and the loop that trains it: this is the next section.
